catalog_quote: p. 182: "The stem-initial position does have a special status in much of Bantu C and frequently is noted to be the site of primary stress/accent. This stem-initial prominence effect can be most easily discerned when the tones in a word are all low or all high." fn 6: "Languages where stem-initial stress/accent is documented include Bobangi (Whitehead 1899, p. 5), Londengese (Hulstaert and Goemaere 1984, p. 9), Ntomba (Mamet 1955, p. 11), Bolia (Mamet 1960, p. 16). These authors are careful to distinguish this metrical prominence effect from the tonal system, which is distinct. I suspect that most of the Bantu C languages have stem-initial metrical prominence, but that in many descriptions the prominence effect is masked by tonal effects." fn 23, p. 114: "I speculate that this is related to the fact that prosodically, the phonologies are all left-dominant, with the left-stem edge being prosodically prominent. ... Certainly to derive the stem-initial primary stress effect that is seen in many Bantu C languages, one would want to align a prosodic foot to the left edge of the morphological stem. Within that foot the left most syllable is the stress bearing head." [runs 'effectfromthe' together; s 'effect from the', which is what is quoted.]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for deng1250, so this is the first stress statement held by the project: stem-initial primary stress/accent, distinct from tone, attributed to Hulstaert & Goemaere 1984: 9. Compatible with our earlier reading finding that all open Aequatoria sources describe tone only. Second-hand; the deciding primary text (Hulstaert & Goemaere 1984 p. 9) remains print-only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Londengese is a tone language in which primary stress/accent (metrical prominence) falls on the stem-initial syllable, i.e. the first syllable of the root after the prefixes; Leitch reports this second-hand from Hulstaert & Goemaere 1984, Grammaire du londengese, p. 9, and stresses that these authors keep the prominence effect apart from the tonal system. Elsewhere (fn 23 p. 114; p. 196) he generalizes: Bantu C phonologies are left-dominant, a foot aligned to the left stem edge with its leftmost syllable as the stress-bearing head.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said. Leitch only speculates (fn 7, p. 182) that the prominence can be derived by left-aligning a binary or unbounded foot to the stem edge; no secondary stress reported for Londengese.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Londengese. General caveat (fn 6): in many Bantu C descriptions the prominence effect is 'masked by tonal effects'; the statement is a footnote citation of a print-only grammar, not a first-hand description.
new_statements.identity_note: Leitch's 'Londengese C-80 / Ndengese' is the language of Hulstaert & Goemaere 1984 (Goemaere's 1940 Dutch manuscript, base dialect of the Ngel'e Njale and Weko per the 1985 Annales Aequatoria notice), i.e. Dengese proper (deng1250), not the Indanga variety that Glottolog also files under deng1250, and not the neighbouring Ohendo/Songomeno (song1305).

sources.citation: Jacobs, John & Barthélemy Omeonga. 2002. Texte et lexique indanga (Kɔlɔmɔnyi, Kɔlɛ, Kasaï Oriental). Annales Aequatoria 23: 537-552.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. The only prosodic remark (p. 538) is one sentence on 'accent musical' (tone): the tone melody of some words changes after a preceding final high tone (nkɔi > nkɔ́i 'léopard' in mǎ nkɔ́i). Lexicon (pp. 548-552) sorts verb radicals by tone (ton bas / ton haut). Data from 1954 fieldwork at Kolomonyi (Kole); Indanga is assigned to deng1250 by Glottolog via Motingea 1992.

sources.note: NOT deng1250: Ohendo = Songomeno (song1305, ISO soe), the Ndengese's neighbour (Guthrie grouped it with Kuba; Motingea places it with Nkundo-Mongo). §'Tonologie et syllabation' p. 122: tones and syllable types 'respectent l'allure générale des parlers môngo'; elided-syllable tone projects onto the next syllable.
